en: Title: *Manasvināgarājasūtra Published: Strauch 2014 Source: Bajaur manuscript collection

This constitutes the earliest hard evidence for any *rakṣā* text. The manuscripts from the Bajaur Collection can be dated to the first two centuries of the Common Era. In these texts, the *nāga*-king Manasvin approaches the Buddha and offers him a special mantra to be employed against all manner of calamities. Only five excerpts are published in this article. The author concludes that this text is very close to the *Mahāmāyūrī*, for which a Gāndhārī origin has been postulated based on linguistic arguments.

He must not be caused fear by humans, nor by non-humans, nor by wild animals; he must not be caused fear by serpents, nor by *jatu* [insects], nor by *yakṣas*, nor by those of malicious intent; he must not be subjected to weapons at the wrong time, nor fire be set to him, nor water be poured upon him, nor poison be administered to him...
That is to say, there is no fear from the ten obstacles: kings, thieves, fire, water, humans, non-humans, wild beasts, and snakes.

This indeed is the mind-pleasing *vidyā*. It is to be meditated upon by one who has gone to the path; it is to be meditated upon by one who has entered the city; it is to be meditated upon by one who has entered the royal palace; it is to be meditated upon by one who has entered the royal courtyard; it is to be meditated upon by one who has entered the inner chamber; it is to be meditated upon by one who has entered the non-inner chamber; it is to be meditated upon by one who has entered the weapon-chamber; it is to be meditated upon by one who has entered the fire-chamber; it is to be meditated upon by one who has entered the water-chamber; it is to be meditated upon by one who has been bitten by poison. (Note: This spell is called *vidyā* or *vidyārāja*, but is also referred to as *mantra* [Sanskrit: *mantra*; Pali/Gāndhārī: *matra*] in later texts.)

Q3 (BajC 3, ll. 46–51): “Recite, O Ānanda, the *Manasviya-vijarāja*. Recite, O Ānanda, the *Manasviya-vijarāja*. It will be for the benefit and happiness of the forest-dwelling monks; it will be for the benefit, happiness, and comfortable dwelling of the fourfold assembly—of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. Thus, Blessed One, has this *Ānanda-manasviya* been taught by the Blessed One? ... [the Blessed One] said: ‘Yes, it has been taught. [The assembly] rejoiced at what was spoken by the Blessed One.

Seated, white, with armlets, bracelets, earrings, teeth, beauty, splendor, majesty, and power; (the person who accomplishes the task), having destroyed the three worlds, the three stars, the faces of the ṛṣis, *hili cili khili cili*... (destroyed) the three stars, descended, descended, *dadura*, *daha*, most excellent, well-spoken, most excellent of the most excellent.
% Note: The mantra is recited twice, once by the nāga and once by the Buddha. % Names of the mahāviṣas Q5 (BajC 3, ll. 29–30)
In this very way, Maṇaspīya, in this very way, Maṇaspīya—[in this very way], Maṇaspīya—one should not fear those men who pay homage to these great deities.
